question: Can triggered abilities trigger on an opponent's turn without Reaction?
answer: Yes. Whenever their condition is met, triggered abilities are added to the chain as pending items, regardless of whose turn it is. [ 383.3 ] [ 383.3.c ] The Reaction keyword is not required for this to work on an opponent's turn. Unlike spells and activated abilities which require Reaction to be played outside your turn, satisfying a trigger condition automatically creates the pending ability. That ability must still finalize: it may be removed if its controller declines an initial "you may," if legal choices are unavailable, or if a required trigger cost is not paid. [ 383.3.a.2 ] [ 402.4 ] [ 404.2 ] Example Blade Dancer triggers when you choose a friendly unit. This can happen on your opponent's turn, for example when you play a Reaction spell that targets one of your own units.

question: Can I react to triggered and activated abilities?
answer: Yes, with one important exception: abilities that use the Add keyword. All triggered and activated abilities are placed on the chain. [ 377.3 ] [ 383.3 ] However, abilities that add resources resolve immediately when finalized, which means players do not receive priority to react to them. [ 337.2 ] [ 429.2 ] [ 429.2.a ]

question: Does removing a triggered ability's source stop that ability?
answer: Usually no — once a triggered ability has finalized, removing its source does not remove or counter the ability on the chain. [ 383.3 ] [ 406.2 ] The ability still resolves and executes its instructions like a spell. [ 406.5 ] To stop the chain item itself, an effect must specifically instruct a player to counter it. [ 425.2.a ] [ 425.3 ] However, removing the source can prevent an instruction from working if it needs information from that source. Source referents such as "here," "my," or "this battlefield" are checked when the instruction executes. [ 359.3.f.1 ] [ 359.3.f.2 ] If the source is no longer on the board, information such as its location is unavailable, and an instruction that needs that information is ignored. [ 359.3.e.6 ] [ 359.3.e.12 ] Examples If an opponent responds to Ashe, Focused 's play effect with Star-Crossed and returns Ashe to her owner's hand, her ability still resolves. Nothing in its instructions requires Ashe to remain on the board. If Star-Crossed returns Vi, Peacekeeper before her attack trigger resolves, Vi cannot Stun an enemy unit "here." Because Vi is no longer on the board, she has no location for "here" to reference, so that instruction is ignored. The same applies to Azir, Sovereign : if Azir leaves the board before his attack trigger resolves, there is no "this battlefield" to which his token units can move.

question: When does the game check an "if" condition in a triggered ability?
answer: It depends on where the condition appears in the ability's text. The trigger condition begins with "When," "At," or "The [Nth] time" and includes the event and any qualifiers attached to it. [ 383.2.a ] An additional conditional statement immediately following that condition is also part of the trigger condition, even if it appears after a comma. [ 383.2.a.1 ] The remaining instructions form the ability's effect. [ 383.2.b ] Every requirement in the trigger condition must be satisfied for the ability to be placed on the chain. For example, Sunken Temple reads "When you conquer here with one or more Mighty units, you may pay 1 to draw 1." The requirement that the conquering units be Mighty is embedded in the trigger condition; if no Mighty unit participated in the conquer, the ability does not trigger. An "if" clause that immediately follows the trigger condition is therefore part of that condition and checked when the triggering event occurs. If the condition is not satisfied at the moment the triggering event occurs, the ability is never placed on the chain at all. [ 383.2.a.1 ] However, "if" clauses embedded within the effect text — coming after an effect instruction rather than immediately following the trigger condition — are only checked on resolution. The ability goes on the chain regardless, and the condition is only evaluated when it resolves. Example Gutter Palace reads "At the start of your Beginning Phase, if you have exactly 4 cards in hand and exactly 4 units at battlefields, you win the game." The "if" clause immediately follows the trigger condition, so it is part of that condition and checked when the triggering event occurs. This ability is only placed on the chain if you already have exactly 4 cards in hand and exactly 4 units at battlefields at the start of your Beginning Phase. If the condition is not satisfied at that moment, the ability does not trigger at all. Example Loose Cannon reads "At start of your Beginning Phase, draw 1 if you have one or fewer cards in your hand." Here the "if" clause does not immediately follow the trigger condition — it comes after the effect instruction "draw 1". This means it is part of the effect and is checked on resolution. The ability goes on the chain at the start of every one of your Beginning Phases, regardless of how many cards are in your hand. Only when the ability resolves is the hand size checked; if you have more than one card at that point, the draw does not happen.

question: When do I choose whether to use a triggered ability that says "you may"?
answer: It depends on where "you may" appears in the ability's effect. If "you may" is the first part of the effect, you decide whether to perform the ability during finalization. [ 383.3.a ] [ 402.1 ] If you decline, the pending ability is removed from the chain and considered not to have triggered. [ 383.3.a.2 ] [ 402.1.a ] If you accept, you make all choices required for finalization and pay any costs incurred during finalization before the ability can finalize. [ 402.2 ] [ 404 ] If "you may" appears later in the effect, you decide whether to perform that instruction when the ability resolves. [ 383.3.a.3 ]

question: When do I pay a cost in a triggered ability that says "you may"?
answer: It depends on where the cost appears in the triggered ability's effect. In rules text phrased as "[do X] to [do Y]," the [do X] part is considered a cost within instructions. If that cost appears at the beginning of a triggered effect or immediately after an initial "you may," it becomes the ability's base cost and must be paid during finalization. [ 383.3.b ] [ 383.3.b.1 ] [ 740.4.a.2 ] [ 403.1.b.1 ] If you decline to pay, the pending ability is removed from the chain without finalizing. [ 404.2 ] If the cost appears later in the triggered effect, you pay it when the ability resolves. [ 740.4.a.2.a ] Example Vayne, Hunter 's ability reads "When I conquer, you may pay 1 to return me to my owner's hand." It will trigger when you conquer. At finalization, you must decide whether to pay the 1 cost. If you decline, the pending ability is removed from the chain. If you pay, the ability finalizes and opponents have the opportunity to react before it resolves.

question: Can I react to units being played?
answer: No, as units enter the board immediately without priority being passed to other players. Unlike spells, units resolve the moment they are finalized and do not open a window of opportunity for reactions. [ 337.2 ] [ 359.2 ] If the unit has a play effect ("When you play me…"), or if another permanent's triggered ability fires as it enters the board, those triggered abilities are placed on the chain as pending items after the unit has already entered. [ 383.4.a.2 ] [ 383.2.c ] [ 383.3 ] Once those pending items are finalized with no further items pending, priority passes and players may react [ 337.4 ] — but by that point, the unit is already in play.

question: In what order are multiple pending chain items finalized and resolved?
answer: Pending items are finalized in the order they were added, starting with the oldest. [ 337.1 ] [ 337.1.b ] A unit, gear, or ability that adds resources resolves immediately when it finalizes. [ 337.2 ] Other finalized items remain on the chain while the remaining pending items are processed. Players do not receive priority until no pending items remain. [ 337.3 ] [ 337.4 ] After players pass priority, finalized chain items resolve in the opposite direction, starting with the newest. [ 340.1 ]

question: Can I play a reaction after one, but not all, items on the chain have resolved?
answer: Yes, once you have gained priority. The chain does not have to resolve in its entirety prior to (re)gaining priority, unlike in some other TCGs. Any time the most recent item on the chain resolves and there are no pending items, the controller of the newest item on the chain gains priority. [ 340.4 ] Example You put Singularity on the chain targeting an opponent's unit. Your opponent reacts by putting their Wind Wall on the chain, attempting to counter the Singularity. In response, you play Stupefy , in the hopes of drawing into a counterspell of your own. Once Stupefy resolves and you draw a card, priority is back to your opponent as the most recent item is their Wind Wall. After they pass priority, you can react once again and play your own counterspell, assuming you drew it off of the Stupefy.

question: Outside a showdown, do I lose control of a battlefield as soon as my last unit leaves it?
answer: No, not immediately. Outside a showdown, control of an empty battlefield is checked during a cleanup, not at the moment the last unit leaves. You lose control only if the battlefield is still empty and the turn is in an open state. [ 190.4.c ] [ 323.6 ] If the chain still contains an item when a cleanup occurs, the turn is in a closed state and you keep control through that cleanup. [ 309.1 ] You can lose control during a later cleanup after the turn returns to an open state if the battlefield remains empty.

question: Are paid costs refunded if a card or ability is countered?
answer: No. Countering does not refund any costs paid to play a card, activate an ability, or trigger an ability, including additional costs. question: What are optional additional costs?
answer: Optional additional costs are additional costs a player may choose to pay. [ 356.2.b.1 ] Their rules text uses both "may" and the exact phrase "as an additional cost." Accelerate and Repeat are keyworded optional additional costs. [ 805.1.a ] [ 820.1.d ] The player chooses whether to pay an optional additional cost while making relevant choices. If chosen, it is included while determining the card's total cost before applicable discounts are applied. [ 355.1.a ] [ 356.2 ] [ 356.4 ]

question: What costs still apply when I play a card ignoring its cost?
answer: Additional costs and cost increases still apply. Playing a card "ignoring its cost" sets only its base energy and power costs to zero. [ 356.1.b.1 ] Additional costs and cost increases are applied afterward and can raise its total cost above zero. [ 356.1.b.3 ] Mandatory additional costs must still be paid, while optional additional costs may still be chosen and paid. [ 356.2.a.1 ] [ 356.2.b.1 ] By contrast, "ignoring any and all costs" sets the card's total cost to zero, including non-standard costs. [ 356.5.a ]

question: Can players react while costs are being paid?
answer: Not through a normal reaction window. Costs are paid while the card or ability is being finalized, and finalization does not pass priority. [ 357 ] [ 404 ] [ 337.1.a ] When resources are required, the player paying them may activate eligible Add abilities with Reaction during that payment. [ 429.3 ] [ 444.2.c ] This is a special permission for resource payment, not a normal reaction window: those abilities finalize and resolve immediately without passing priority. [ 429.2 ] [ 429.2.a ] Any normal opportunity to react comes only after finalization, when the costs have already been paid.

question: Does a unit move when it enters the board?
answer: No. Moving means changing a permanent's position from one space on the board to another. [ 446.1 ] A card entering the board from another game zone is a zone change, not a move. question: What does "play" mean on a card?
answer: "Play" refers to the same underlying action, but rules text uses it in three contexts that initiate or check that action at different points. [ 419.1 ] [ 419.4 ] In trigger conditions — "When you play," as seen on Ravenbloom Student and Darius, Trifarian — it means resolve. A card is Played once the entire process of playing it is complete, and these abilities trigger when that happens at the card's resolution. [ 350.1 ] [ 419.4.a ] For units and gear, that's the instant they're finalized, since both resolve immediately without priority being passed; [ 337.2 ] for spells, resolution is a separate, later step, reached only after finalization and any reactions have played out. [ 339.1 ] [ 340.1 ] In conditional statements checking whether a card has been played — "if you've played," as seen on Battering Ram , Crescent Guardian , and Back Off — it means finalize, not resolve. Although the rules call these "non-triggered abilities," an ability can be part of a game object or spell, so this includes conditions checked while a spell's instructions resolve. [ 361 ] [ 419.4.b ] A card satisfies this check when its pending chain item becomes a finalized chain item. [ 329.3 ] The Legion keyword makes this precise: it's written as "if you have played another card this turn," [ 812.1.b.1 ] but the dependent ability is active as long as that other card "has been Finalized by you on the same turn" — not resolved. [ 812.1.c ] As an instruction — "play a card," as seen on Here to Help and Fizz, Trickster — it initiates that underlying action by placing the card on the chain and queuing it for finalization. [ 419.1 ] When a game effect instructs a player to play a card during its resolution, that play follows all the normal steps unless the effect says otherwise. [ 419.3 ] [ 419.3.b ] Hiding is a separate action that puts a card facedown at a battlefield, so it does not satisfy an instruction to play that card. [ 421.1 ] [ 811.1.c.1 ]

question: When does a card leave my trash when I play it from there?
answer: As soon as you begin playing it. The first step of playing a card moves it from its current zone to the chain, where it waits to be finalized. [ 354 ] [ 354.2 ] Once you begin playing a card from your trash, it is no longer there while you make choices, determine its total cost, or resolve it. If the card counts copies of itself in your trash, only the other copies still there count. Likewise, if its cost is reduced for each card in your trash, it does not count itself toward that reduction.

question: When does a showdown close?
answer: Under normal game procedure, a showdown does not close abruptly. It ends once all players have consecutively passed focus on an empty chain. [ 348 ] Example You control a battlefield with a 2 might Stalwart Poro on it. Your opponent moves their Ravenbloom Student into that battlefield starting a showdown. When combat opens, Stalwart Poro becomes a defender and its Shield increases its might to 3. Once your opponent gains focus, they play Hextech Ray targeting Stalwart Poro. Hextech Ray resolves, marking 3 damage on it. During the resulting cleanup, Stalwart Poro is killed for lethal damage. [ 323.5 ] The showdown does not end right away and you gain focus as usual. You still have the opportunity to play a legally timed card or ability in an attempt to prevent your opponent from conquering. [ 347.1 ]

question: What happens if another player's unit moves into an existing non-combat showdown?
answer: When a unit controlled by a different player becomes present during a non-combat showdown, combat is staged and the showdown becomes a combat showdown during the cleanup following that unit's arrival. [ 316.8.b.1.a ] [ 323.9 ] [ 323.14 ] As combat opens, the player who originally applied contested status to the battlefield becomes the attacker, [ 464.2.c.1 ] and the player who moves in during the showdown becomes the defender. [ 464.2.c.2 ] Their units at that battlefield receive the corresponding designations then, [ 464.2.c.3 ] enabling combat-related keywords such as Assault and Shield and causing attack or defend triggers to happen. This interaction is commonly called the surprise defender: the player who first contested the battlefield remains the attacker, while the player joining later becomes the defender.

question: When do attack and defend triggers happen?
answer: Attack and defend triggered abilities (such as "When I attack" or "When I defend") trigger when a unit receives its attacker or defender designation, not necessarily at the start of combat. Units already present receive their initial designations when combat opens. [ 464.2.c.3 ] Units that join an ongoing combat receive their designations during the cleanup following their arrival.

question: Units can join combat late and still trigger
answer: If a unit is moved into a battlefield where combat is already in progress, it will receive the appropriate attacker or defender designation during the next cleanup. [ 323.2.a ] When it receives this designation, any "When I attack" or "When I defend" abilities will trigger at that time.

question: Can attack and defend abilities trigger more than once per combat?
answer: Attack and defend triggered abilities can only trigger once per combat, even if a unit gains and loses its designation multiple times. [ 383.4.e.2.a ] [ 383.4.f.2.a ] Once a unit has been assigned an attacker or defender designation during a combat, moving it away from the battlefield will cause it to lose that designation. [ 323.2.c ] If that unit is moved back to the same battlefield during the same combat, it will gain the same designation as its controller, [ 323.2.a ] which will be the same designation it previously had. However, its "When I attack" or "When I defend" ability will not trigger again, as these abilities can only be fulfilled once per combat.

question: What makes something a target?
answer: Unless one of the exceptions below applies, a game object, player, or zone mentioned by a spell or ability is a target. [ 355.7 ] [ 355.10 ] All targets are declared during finalization. [ 355.8 ] Card text does not need to use the word "target" or "choose" explicitly — targeting can be implied, as in "Kill a unit" or "Move a friendly unit." Abilities that reference "when you choose" a game object, such as Irelia, Fervent 's "When you choose or ready me, give me +1 Might this turn," are specifically triggered when being targeted. [ 383.4.b.3 ] When in doubt, assume it is a target — the list below covers the only situations where it is not: It is in a non-public zone (hand, main deck, etc.) [ 355.10.a ] e.g., "You may play a unit from your hand" does not target a unit — it merely lets you play one. It is only a location requirement for another target . [ 355.10.b ] Words like "at a battlefield" narrow down which objects are valid targets; the battlefield itself is not a target — unless the effect lets you choose which of several battlefields to affect, as in "Kill all units at a battlefield." It is part of a trigger condition, cost, or replacement effect . [ 355.10.c ] [ 355.10.c.1 ] Objects referenced in "when X happens" conditions, payment costs (see also When do I pay a cost in a triggered ability that says "you may"? ), or "instead" effects are not targets. e.g., the dying unit in "When a friendly unit dies, kill a gear" is not a target — only the gear is. There is no real choice involved . [ 355.10.d ] If an effect applies to every object meeting a description rather than a specific one you pick, nothing is targeted. e.g., "Kill all units at battlefields" targets nothing because you are not choosing among individual units. This applies only when a choice is never possible — not when an object merely happens to be the only valid choice right now: "Kill a unit at a battlefield" still targets a unit even if only one unit is there. [ 355.10.d.1 ] [ 355.10.d.2 ] It is part of a set chosen wholly or partly by other players . [ 355.10.e ] Objects chosen this way are not targets, even if the spell or ability's controller also chooses part of the set. e.g., "Each player kills a unit they control" targets nothing — each player chooses their unit as the effect resolves. The instruction uses "must" . [ 355.10.f ] This signals the choice is made on resolution rather than upfront. e.g., "You must recycle one of your runes" does not target, whereas "Recycle a rune you control" does.

question: Does "Kill a unit if it has 3 might or less" mean I can only choose a unit with 3 might or less?
answer: No. Only words that describe the target restrict which objects can be chosen. For example, "Kill a unit with 3 might or less" can target only a unit meeting that description. [ 355.9.b ] A separate condition on an effect does not restrict its targets. "Kill a unit if it has 3 might or less" can target any otherwise legal unit; the might condition is checked when that instruction resolves.

question: What happens if a target becomes illegal before a spell or ability resolves?
answer: The illegal target is unaffected, but the spell or ability still resolves. Instructions related to that target cannot be followed, while independent instructions continue normally. [ 359.3.e.5 ] [ 359.3.e.6 ] If an instruction needs information from the illegal target, that information is null and calculations using it are ignored. [ 359.3.e.12 ] If a later instruction is linked to an earlier instruction that was ignored, the later instruction is also ignored. [ 359.3.e.14.a ]

question: Can I use Ambush to play a unit to my base?
answer: No. Ambush only permits playing a unit to a battlefield; it has no effect on your base. Ambush is shorthand for "I may be played to a battlefield where you control units" and "I have Reaction as long as I'm being played to a battlefield where you control units." [ 822.1.b ] The permission Ambush grants is strictly limited to battlefields — a base is not a battlefield, so Ambush never makes it a valid destination. [ 822.1.c ] Playing a unit to your base is already permitted by the default rules for valid locations, [ 355.2.a ] but choosing base does not grant the unit Reaction . It can be played there only at its normal timing.

question: Can opponents react to a unit being played with Ambush?
answer: No. Ambush grants the unit Reaction speed, which determines when it can be played — it does not create a window for opponents to respond before the unit enters. Units resolve the moment they are finalized without entering the Execute step, [ 337.2 ] and finalization does not pass priority. [ 337.1.a ] The unit enters the board immediately, just as any unit played during an open state would (see also Can I react to units being played? ). This is a common point of confusion with cards like Kha'Zix, Mutating Horror , which has Ambush and triggers if an enemy unit is alone when he attacks or defends. An opponent cannot play a unit in response to Kha'Zix being placed on the chain in an attempt to break the "alone" condition before he enters.

question: Who gets to act after I Ambush a unit during a showdown?
answer: It depends on whether anything else remains on the chain once the unit enters. When played onto an empty chain, the unit enters immediately, the chain empties, and the turn returns to an open state during the showdown — focus passes to the next player in turn order. [ 340.2.a ] This catches many players off guard — you move in to attack, Ambush a unit, and expect to retain focus, but your opponent gets to act first. When played in response to something already on the chain — such as attack or defend triggers, or a spell — the turn does not return to an open state after the unit resolves, so focus does not pass. [ 346 ] Priority instead passes to the controller of the newest remaining item on the chain. [ 340.4 ]

question: When is a Deathknell ability added to the chain?
answer: A Deathknell ability is added to the chain as a pending item before the dying permanent moves to the trash. [ 808.1.d.2 ] Before the permanent leaves the board, the game records its location, attributes, and other information needed by its ability. [ 808.1.d.3 ] If the permanent's death is replaced and it is not sent to the trash, the pending ability is removed from the chain. [ 808.1.d.1 ] Each instance of Deathknell triggers separately and creates its own pending item. [ 808.2 ] [ 808.2.a ]

question: When does a Deathknell ability resolve if its unit dies during a cleanup?
answer: After the cleanup finishes. The ability becomes a pending item before the unit moves to the trash. [ 323.4 ] [ 323.5 ] [ 808.1.d.2 ] The remaining cleanup steps are then completed before that pending ability can be finalized. [ 334 ] During a combat cleanup, this means surviving units are healed before the Deathknell ability is finalized or resolved. [ 466.1.a.1 ] After the cleanup, the ability is finalized, any required targets are chosen, and players receive priority before it resolves. [ 334.2 ] [ 337.4 ]

question: Does Deathknell resolve before the card or ability that killed the unit?
answer: It depends on when the unit is killed and what kind of chain item caused it.

question: Killed as a cost
answer: If a unit is killed to pay a cost, the kill happens while the card or ability is being finalized. [ 357.2 ] [ 404.1 ] The Deathknell ability becomes pending above that chain item. [ 808.1.d.2 ] If the original item is a spell or an ability that does not add resources, the pending Deathknell ability is finalized before play continues. [ 359.3.b ] [ 406.3 ] Because it is newer on the chain, the Deathknell ability resolves before that spell or ability. [ 340.1 ] If the original item is a unit, gear, or ability that adds resources, it resolves immediately when finalized, before the pending Deathknell ability is processed. [ 337.2 ] The Deathknell ability resolves afterward.

question: Killed during resolution
answer: If a resolving card or ability kills the unit, that chain item continues resolving without interruption. [ 354.3 ] The Deathknell ability becomes pending, but it cannot be finalized until the current chain item finishes resolving. [ 334.2 ] The killing card or ability therefore finishes before the Deathknell ability can resolve.

question: Can opponents react to an Empower ability?
answer: Yes. Empower is an activated ability keyword, [ 827.1 ] and activated abilities use the chain. [ 377.3 ] After the ability is finalized, opponents have an opportunity to react before it resolves. [ 377.3.b.2 ] This differs from activated abilities that use Add , which resolve immediately when finalized and cannot be reacted to. [ 337.2 ] [ 429.2 ] See also Can I react to triggered and activated abilities? .

question: When can I activate an Empower ability?
answer: By default, only during your own Main Phase while the turn is in a neutral open state. An Empower ability is an activated ability, [ 827.1 ] and activated abilities can normally be activated only on their controller's turn during an open state. [ 381 ] Because Empower has neither Action nor Reaction by default, it cannot be activated during a showdown or in response to another chain item. [ 308.1.a ] [ 309.1.a ] An Empower ability may have text that changes its timing. [ 827.1.c.4 ] If it explicitly has Action or Reaction , follow the permissions of that keyword instead.

question: Does a "When I become Empowered" ability trigger if the unit leaves the board before its Empower ability resolves?
answer: No. If the unit is killed, returned to hand, or otherwise leaves the board before its Empower ability resolves, it does not become Empowered and its "When I become Empowered " ability does not trigger. The Empower ability remains on the chain, but the Empowered state exists only for game objects on the board. [ 441.2 ] Because triggered abilities of permanents can evaluate their conditions only while their source is on the board, its dependent "When I become Empowered " ability is not active and does not trigger. [ 384.2 ] [ 828.1.c ] [ 828.1.d ] Example A player activates Mel, Defiant Soul 's Empower ability by discarding a spell. An opponent responds with Star-Crossed and returns Mel to her owner's hand. When the Empower ability resolves, Mel is no longer a game object on the board and does not become Empowered . Her "When I become Empowered " ability does not trigger, so no enemy unit is banished.

question: Can a unit or gear without an Empower or Empowered ability become Empowered?
answer: Yes, if a game effect instructs a player to empower it. The Empowered state can apply to game objects on the board; it is not restricted to cards with printed Empower or Empowered abilities. [ 441.1 ] [ 441.2 ] Players cannot empower a game object at will, however; they may do so only when directed by a game effect. [ 441.3 ] [ 441.3.a ] Examples Sanction can empower any unit that is a legal choice, even if that unit has no printed reference to Empower or Empowered . Once that unit is Empowered , effects such as Aurok General 's ability can identify and affect it normally. Hextech Formula can empower another gear, even if that gear has no printed reference to Empower or Empowered .

question: What happens to attached equipment when a unit dies?
answer: The equipment detaches and remains at the unit's last location, recalling if at a battlefield. When a unit with attached equipment dies, the equipment detaches and remains at the location the unit occupied before dying. [ 719.5 ] [ 435.4.b ] If that location is a battlefield, the detached equipment will be recalled to its controller's base during the next cleanup. [ 435.4.a ] If that location is the controller's base, the equipment simply remains there.

question: What happens to attached equipment when you take control of an enemy unit?
answer: Equipment stays attached but its controller does not change — only the top-most unit's controller changes. When you take control of a unit, any equipment attached to it retains its current controller. Changes in control of the top-most card do not affect control of attached cards, and vice versa. [ 718.5.f ] When the equipment detaches, it remains at the unit's last location. [ 719.5 ] [ 435.4.b ] If that location is a battlefield, it is recalled to its controller's base during the next cleanup. [ 435.4.a ] If that location is another player's base, the equipment remains there until the next cleanup, when it is recalled to its controller's base. [ 323.7 ] Because the equipment remains under the other player's control, that player can play a unit with Weaponmaster and choose the equipment, even while it is attached to the unit you control. [ 718.5.b ] [ 821.1.c ] If its Equip cost can be paid and it can legally be detached and attached, it moves to the newly played unit. [ 821.1.c.4 ] [ 821.1.c.5 ]

question: Do Equip, Quick-Draw, or Weaponmaster count as choosing a unit?
answer: Equip and Quick-Draw choose units; Weaponmaster does not. Some abilities trigger or care about when you choose friendly units. Here's how equipment-related effects interact with such abilities: When you activate a gear's Equip ability, you choose a unit you control to attach the equipment to. [ 818.1.b.1 ] This choice is a target, so activating Equip counts as choosing a unit. [ 355.7 ] When you play a gear with Quick-Draw , its triggered ability instructs you to "attach it to a Unit you control". [ 819.1.d ] While attaching cards doesn't inherently choose or specify a target, [ 434.3 ] Quick-Draw 's ability does require you to choose which unit to attach to. [ 355.10 ] This counts as choosing a unit. When you play a unit with Weaponmaster , you choose an equipment you control, not the unit. [ 821.1.c ] The rules explicitly state that "The Equip ability is not activated this way, and the unit with the Weaponmaster ability is not chosen". [ 821.1.c.6 ] Therefore, Weaponmaster does not count as choosing a unit.

question: Can opponents react to Equip, Quick-Draw, or Weaponmaster abilities?
answer: Yes — all three equipment-related abilities create chain items that opponents can respond to before the attachment resolves. Equip is an activated ability. [ 818.1 ] Activated abilities use the chain, [ 377.3 ] so when you activate Equip , opponents have an opportunity to play a Reaction spell or ability before the attachment resolves. [ 377.3.b.2 ] When you play a Quick-Draw gear, the gear itself resolves immediately when finalized and cannot be reacted to. [ 337.2 ] However, Quick-Draw 's triggered ability — "When you play this, attach it to a unit you control" [ 819.1.d ] — is placed on the chain as a separate item. [ 383.4.a.2 ] Opponents can respond to that ability before the attachment resolves. Weaponmaster is also a triggered ability keyword. [ 821.1 ] Its ability triggers when you play the unit, and is placed on the chain just like any other triggered ability. [ 383.4.a.2 ] Opponents can respond to it before the equipment is attached. Skipping straight to attaching without checking for reactions is not correct play for any of these abilities.

question: When can I play a spell using Flow?
answer: You can play it only when its existing timing restrictions allow. Flow lets you play the spell from your trash for its Flow cost, but it changes no other permissions or timing restrictions. [ 829.1.b ] [ 829.1.b.2 ] For example, Flow does not grant a spell Reaction or let you play an Action outside its normal timing.

question: Where does a spell played using Flow go if it is countered?
answer: It is banished unless another replacement effect changes that result. Countering clears the spell from the chain and would normally put it in the trash. [ 425.1.a ] [ 425.1.a.1 ] However, playing a spell using Flow creates a delayed replacement effect that banishes it if it would leave the chain after becoming finalized, unless its own execution instructed it to leave. [ 829.1.b.1 ] Being countered meets those conditions, so the Flow replacement effect banishes the spell instead of letting it go to the trash.

question: Can Defy counter a spell whose Flow cost exceeds Defy's limit?
answer: Yes, provided the spell's printed cost meets Defy's restrictions. Defy checks the cost of its target, and effects that determine a card's cost always use its printed or copied cost rather than the amount actually paid. [ 206 ] A Flow cost is an alternate cost that replaces the spell's base cost during finalization, [ 829.1.c.1 ] but it does not change the printed cost that Defy checks. Example Lacerate has a printed cost of 2 and a Flow cost of 4 . Defy can counter it because Defy checks the printed cost, not the Flow cost paid.

question: Where does a Flow spell countered by Abandon go?
answer: It is banished rather than returned to its owner's hand. Abandon replaces putting the countered spell in the trash with returning it to its owner's hand, while Flow replaces the spell leaving the chain with banishing it. [ 425.1.a.1 ] [ 829.1.b.1 ] Because both replacement effects apply to the affected spell's departure from the chain, that spell's controller chooses their order. [ 372 ] The result is the same in either order. If Flow applies first, the spell is banished instead of going to the trash, so Abandon no longer has a qualifying event to replace. If Abandon applies first, it still replaces the original event with the spell leaving the chain for its owner's hand, so Flow applies to that replacement event and banishes the spell instead. [ 370.2 ] How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 31 July 2026 .

question: When do I decide whether to pay for Repeat?
answer: You must decide whether to pay a spell's Repeat cost when you play the spell, not later. When you play a spell with Repeat , you follow the normal process for playing a card: [ 353 ] First, you put the spell onto the chain [ 354 ] Then, you make relevant choices, [ 355 ] including whether or not you will pay its Repeat cost [ 355.1 ] [ 820.1.d ] Next, you determine its total cost. [ 356 ] If you chose to pay it, you apply the Repeat cost as an optional additional cost. [ 356.2.b.1 ] [ 820.1.d ] Finally, you complete the remaining steps of playing the card to finalize the spell This means you cannot put a spell on the chain, pass priority to see what happens, and then decide whether to pay its Repeat cost later. The decision must be made upfront during finalization. Any targets, modes, or other choices for the additional execution are also made during finalization and may differ from the original execution's choices. [ 820.2 ] [ 820.2.a ] Example You put Blood Rush , a spell with Repeat 1 , that says "Give a unit Assault 2 this turn," onto the chain. Before anyone can respond, you must decide whether to pay the 1 Repeat cost and choose the target for each execution. The two targets may be the same unit or different units. Once you've made this choice and paid costs, the spell is finalized. Your opponent can now respond with priority, but your Repeat decision is locked in.

question: What does Repeat repeat?
answer: Repeat executes a spell or ability's instructions an additional time during resolution; it does not create another copy or chain item. [ 820.1.d.1 ] [ 820.3.a ] The spell or ability is played only once, so its costs are paid only once during its original finalization. Targets, modes, and other choices are made separately for each execution. [ 820.2 ] [ 820.2.a ] Those choices may differ between the original and additional executions.

question: What happens if a spell with Repeat is countered?
answer: The entire spell is countered, including all repeated instructions. Repeat does not create a second instance of the spell on the chain. [ 820.3.a ] Instead, it modifies how the spell resolves by executing its instructions an additional time. [ 820.1.d.1 ] When a spell is countered, it does nothing and is cleared from the chain. [ 425.1.a ] Since the spell never resolves, none of its instructions are executed, whether they came from Repeat or not.
